newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Little shine seen in Central Asian gold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Little shine seen in Central Asian gold.

text.p: Low prices, high risks and fallout from Indonesia's Busang scandal have caused foreign investors to shy away from gold deposits laying beneath the Central Asian deserts and mountains, industry sources said on Monday.
Kyrgyzstan's state gold concern, Kyrgyzaltyn, said on Monday it would explore territory in the south of the former Soviet republic with U.S. mining company Phelps Dodge Corp.
But the $5 million to be spent on the project is considered small for the region's gold-rich republics.
"The Bre-X scandal is a big factor in why there's so little activity in Central Asia," said a representative of a Canadian-owned gold junior here, who declined to be named.
Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd caused a furor when an independent audit showed its Busang property in Indonesia, touted as the biggest find this century, worthless.
"It's very difficult to get cash on the Canadian stock exchanges now," the representative said.
The collapse in gold prices to 12-year lows to under $320 an ounce has also cooled interest.

"Kazakhstan could be among the top 20 gold producers in the world," said Alexander Lesser, a Kazakhstan-based lawyer who advises mining companies in Central Asia. "But the region is remote, unfamiliar and the low gold price won't help," he said.

A London-based gold analyst, speaking on condition of anonymity, said "throughout the region, there's very good geology ,and there's good data on reserves. But the political risk is still viewed as large."
She said "there are bureaucratic hassles, and exporting gold production is a big issue."
Mining companies in the region face difficulties in shipping gold, a confused legal climate and sometimes, violence.
Guerillas in Tajikstan captured two expatriates working for London-based Gold and Mineral Excavation Ltd late last year.

Canadian-listed Nelson Gold Corporation Ltd halted operations at its Zeravshan mine in Tajikistan, now emerging from a four-year civil war, for many months when the government refused to let the firm export production. The dispute was settled, but the export issue has kept mining executives at bay.

Canada's Cameco Corp, developing its world class Kumtor deposit in Kyrgyzstan with reserves of 514 tonnes, and U.S.-based Newmont Mining Corp, producing about a tonne of gold a month at its Zarafshan Newmont project in Uzbekistan, are the only large mining companies operating in the region.
But Richard Wilkins, director of British-based Oxus Resources Corporation which is exploring and producing in four Central Asian republics, is bullish.
"The junior activity in Kazakhstan is buzzing," said Wilkins, whose firm plans an exchange listing in the autumn.
He said Kazakhstan was most attractive to junior mining companies as the mining sector had been effectively privatised.
But mining executives said government corruption and earlier failed deals have scared off potential investors in Kazakhstan.
Heavy-handed governments in other Central Asian states have also meant only the biggest mining companies have ventured in.
Uzbekistan, which produced 71 tonnes of gold last year according to London-based Gold Fields Minerals Services, plans to double production in 5-6 years.
It is tendering seven gold fields with total reserves of 1,720 tonnes of gold to bidders including Britain's Rio Tinto Plc, formerly RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd, and Canada's Mazarin Mining Corp.
But negotiations have crawled on for over a year without results. "It's just too early to invest large amounts of capital (in Central Asia)," said the analyst.
